Dena'ina Ełnena is the land of the Dena'ina, an Athabaskan people of the Cook Inlet region of south-central Alaska, where Anchorage now stands. They are the only northern Athabaskans whose land reached the sea, and they hunted beluga and seals as well as moose and caribou, and fished the great salmon runs.

Their neighbours were the Alutiiq on the outer coast and the Ahtna to the east. James Cook sailed into the inlet in 1778, and Russian traders built a post at Kenai in 1791, part of Russian America. After the Alaska Purchase of 1867, canneries came, and in 1914 the railway town of Anchorage was founded on their land. Several Dena'ina villages, such as Eklutna and Tyonek, remain.
